blocks.title: Order of reaction
blocks.text: The order of a reaction with respect to a specific reactant is the exponent applied to that reactant's concentration in the rate equation. The reaction is of order x with respect to A and y with respect to B, and the overall order is x + y.

The order defines how the reactant concentration influences the rate; for a single reactant it is simply the power of its concentration in the rate equation. Reactions are classified as zero, first, second and third order, and the order gives valuable information about the mechanism. It is crucial to distinguish the order with respect to a single reactant from the overall order. For 2H2(g) + 2NO(g) giving N2(g) + 2H2O(g) the rate law is rate = k [H2][NO]^2: first order with respect to H2, second order with respect to NO, and third order overall (1 + 2 = 3).

blocks.title: Keep in mind
blocks.text: The order of a reaction is the sum of all the exponents to which the concentrations in the rate equation are raised. It is an experimentally determined quantity and cannot be inferred from the reaction equation; the sum of the exponents may or may not equal the sum of the coefficients in the balanced equation.
